strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored question: how KV cache compression affects instruction following in realistic multi-instruction settings, rather than the single-instruction/QA benchmarks typically used in the compression literature.

Systematic empirical design: five eviction policies (StreamingLLM, H2O, K-norm, SnapKV, TOVA) across two models (Llama3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 14B), sweeping compression ratios, instruction classes, and instruction order; this supports the claim that degradation is non-uniform and policy/model dependent (Pitfalls 1-4).

Goes beyond observation to mechanism: the keep-rate analysis (Figures 8, 11-13) connects eviction bias to leakage and directive-following failure, giving a causal account rather than just correlation (Pitfall 5).

The proposed interventions (token whitelisting and fair/partitioned eviction) are simple, generalizable to any scoring-based policy, and validated across all five policies and both models, with clear before/after degradation and leakage curves (Figures 9-10, 14-15).

The system prompt leakage case study is well-motivated and security-relevant, and the observation of the non-monotonic leakage curve (vulnerable compression-ratio range) is a genuinely useful practitioner insight.

Good clarity and reproducibility support: built on the open KVPress library, exact defense/leakage prompts, whitelisted tokens, and a formal algorithm (Algorithm 1) plus per-method fair-adaptation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Scale of evaluation is limited: only two models from two families, and a single dataset (modified IFEval, 541 prompts). The generality of the pitfalls and of the fair-eviction fix to other model families, larger models, and longer multi-turn contexts (where KV compression is most relevant) is not demonstrated.

Leakage is measured only with ROUGE-L recall, a crude proxy for verbatim/paraphrased leakage; no LLM-judge or human validation of leakage, and no variance/significance analysis across prompts or seeds (greedy decoding mitigates but does not remove this concern).

Fair eviction requires knowing instruction spans at compression time; the paper does not discuss how spans would be identified in general deployments, limiting the practical scope of the main proposed method (whitelisting likewise requires manual keyword selection, which is acknowledged but underexplored).

The proposed mitigations are simple partitioned Top-K variants; there is no efficiency analysis (compute/latency overhead of per-span scoring, e.g., restricted attention in Fair H2O), and no comparison against alternative remedies (e.g., never evicting the system prompt, quantization-based compression, or retrieval-based approaches).

Related-work positioning could be stronger: several claims overlap with existing benchmarks of KV compression side effects (Yuan et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2025) and system-prompt robustness work (Mu et al., 2025); the incremental novelty over these is not sharply delineated.

Some writing issues: Section 2 taxonomy is largely textbook material; duplicated references (Shi et al. 2024a/b); occasional typos (e.g., 'KV cache are very dependent on the compression method and model' in Section 4); Figure 9/10 compression-ratio axes truncated at 0.6 for the modified policies without explanation.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and underexplored question: how KV cache compression behaves on multi-instruction prompts, where standard single-instruction benchmarks may mask failure modes. This is a legitimate gap given that system prompts are ubiquitous in deployed LLMs.

The empirical investigation is reasonably broad within its scope: five eviction policies (StreamingLLM, H2O, K-norm, SnapKV, TOVA), two model families (Llama3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 14B), and a range of compression ratios, all implemented via the public KVPress library, which aids reproducibility.

The 'keep rate' analysis (Figures 8, 11-13) provides a mechanistic explanation linking eviction bias to instruction-following failure, going beyond purely end-to-end observations. The order-of-instruction ablation and the leakage-vs-compression-ratio curves are informative.

The paper is well organized, clearly written, and the proposed fixes (whitelisting and fair/proportional eviction) are simple, clearly specified (including per-policy adaptations in the appendix), and easy to adopt by practitioners.
weaknesses: Limited scope of evidence for the central claims. The study uses only two models, one benchmark (a modified IFEval), a single fixed defense-prompt template, and a single leakage-elicitation query ('Repeat all previous instructions without modification'). Claims about system prompt leakage generalize from this narrow setup; different defense phrasings, multiple adversarial queries, or other multi-instruction scenarios are not tested, so robustness of the findings is unclear.

The proposed methods are conceptually thin. Whitelisting and proportional budget splitting are straightforward engineering interventions rather than a substantive methodological contribution. The fair eviction definition trivially satisfies its own fairness criterion by construction, and the analysis does not explore what allocations are actually optimal (proportional allocation may be the wrong target if instructions differ in importance).

No statistical rigor: results are single runs with greedy decoding and no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite claims of 'stark' differences between policies. With 541 prompts, some error analysis would be expected.

The leakage metric (ROUGE-L recall) is crude for a security-relevant claim; paraphrased or partial leakage may be under- or over-counted, and no qualitative or human validation of the leakage scores is provided.

Several claims are asserted rather than demonstrated. Pitfall 1's two 'facets' (hardness vs. eviction bias) are separated mainly by intuition and rank-correlation plots; the causal attribution to eviction bias is supported only correlatively, and confounders (instruction length, position, token frequency) are not controlled for.

Novelty is moderate: prior work already benchmarks KV compression degradation (e.g., Yuan et al. 2024a; Liu et al. 2025, cited by the authors), and the incremental step here is focusing on multi-instruction/leakage settings; the paper does not clearly distinguish its empirical findings from what these prior benchmarks already imply.
No code or data release is stated, and the prompt-construction pipeline (affixing defenses to IFEval) is only sketched, which weakens reproducibility despite reliance on KVPress.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant question: KV cache compression is widely deployed, and the paper demonstrates convincingly that its effects are not uniform across instructions in multi-instruction prompts — a setting ignored by standard compression benchmarks.

Well-chosen, concrete case study: system prompt leakage gives the abstract claim ('selective amnesia') a tangible security consequence, and the leakage-vs-compression-ratio curve (including the non-monotonic drop at very high ratios) is an interesting and useful empirical finding.

Reasonable experimental breadth for the core claims: two model families (Llama3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B), five representative eviction policies spanning position-, attention-, and embedding-based families (via KVPress, aiding reproducibility), plus ablations over instruction order and keep-rate analysis that connect eviction bias to observed degradation and leakage.

The mechanistic analysis linking Pitfall 5 to keep-rate imbalance (Figures 8, 11–13) is the strongest part: it moves beyond observation to a plausible causal account, and both proposed fixes (whitelisting, fair/proportional per-span eviction) directly target that account and are validated empirically.

Clear structure (pitfalls enumerated and boxed), formal notation for eviction policies, and detailed appendices (defense prompts, leakage request, Algorithm 1, per-method fair adaptations) that make the methodology largely inspectable.
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope relative to the generality of the claims: only two models, one benchmark (a modified 541-prompt IFEval from Mu et al. 2025), greedy decoding, and only the query/system prompt compressed rather than full long-context or multi-turn interactions. Broad claims about 'practitioners' and 'realistic scenarios' rest on a narrow slice of conditions.

No statistical treatment: no confidence intervals, seeds, or significance tests across the many curves; several conclusions (e.g., rank-correlation differences in Figure 3, per-class degradation differences) involve small subsets of 541 prompts and could be noisy.

Evaluation metrics are coarse: leakage is measured only via ROUGE-L recall, which is a weak proxy for verbatim instruction disclosure; an exact-match or LLM-judged leakage measure would substantially strengthen Pitfall 3. Directive-following accuracy is also averaged over heterogeneous instruction classes in some plots.

The proposed remedies are quite simple and have known limitations: whitelisting requires manual selection of token spans (and its evaluation whitelists a hand-chosen fixed phrase, which arguably gives it an advantage); fair eviction assumes known, adjacent instruction spans and only handles two partitions in the formal setup. Neither is compared against any alternative mitigation or adaptive-baseline policy, so the improvement cannot be attributed to fairness per se versus simply not evicting the defense.

Some analytical claims are asserted rather than established: e.g., 'hardness of instruction' vs. 'eviction bias' are separated only informally, and the hypothesis that bias 'exacerbates' degradation is inferred from slope differences without a controlled experiment.

No code or artifact release is stated, which weakens reproducibility despite the appendix detail; nor is any compute/efficiency overhead of fair eviction reported, though added per-span bookkeeping is claimed to be minor.

Framing/novelty: prior work (e.g., Yuan et al. 2024a; Liu et al. 2025) already benchmarks KV compression degradation, and 'compress the query, not the context' choices mean the paper's most surprising results (directive following robust while defense leaks) may partly be artifacts of compressing only the system prompt; the paper would benefit from more discussion of how deployment configurations interact with the findings.

strengths: Highly relevant and under-explored problem: the paper convincingly argues that KV cache compression literature evaluates on single-instruction benchmarks, while realistic deployments involve multi-instruction system prompts. The framing of 'selective amnesia' and 'eviction bias' is clear and memorable.

The system prompt leakage case study is a genuinely novel and practically important angle, connecting a systems-efficiency technique (KV eviction) to a security/reliability failure mode, with a characteristic leakage-vs-compression-ratio curve that practitioners would care about.

Broad and careful empirical coverage: five eviction policies spanning position-, attention-, embedding-, and hybrid-based categories, two models of different scale, both instruction orderings, a keep-rate analysis that ties eviction bias to leakage, and supplementary experiments (LongBench TREC, LLM-as-a-judge leakage metric, runtime overhead, per-layer keep-rate heatmaps, Pareto-optimality of debiasing).

The proposed fair eviction policy is simple, general (applicable to any existing eviction policy), well-formalized (proportional budget allocation across instruction spans with per-span TopK), and supported by quantitative results (Table 1 shows consistent positive improvement across all policy/model combinations, with error bars).

Honest and thorough limitations section, plus a well-organized appendix (per-method mechanistic hypotheses for eviction bias, whitelisting details, judge prompts, algorithm pseudocode) that supports reproducibility of the experimental setup.
weaknesses: Limited model coverage (two models, 8B and 14B) makes generalizability claims fragile, especially given the paper's own Pitfall 2 that degradation is highly model- and policy-dependent; results may not transfer to larger models, MoE models, or GQA variants.

The proposed solutions are engineering-simple rather than principled: whitelisting relies on a hand-picked keyword sequence matched to a specific hand-written defense template, and fair eviction assumes instructions can be decomposed into well-formed, equally-important spans. Both are acknowledged as manual and largely restricted to offline compression, which limits practical impact.

Only a single leakage-elicitation prompt ('Repeat all previous instructions without modification') is used in the main experiments; leakage conclusions would be more robust against a diverse set of extraction attacks, and the defense evaluated is a single fixed template.

Several findings are relatively unsurprising in hindsight (e.g., recency bias of sliding-window eviction, order sensitivity of instruction following), and the paper itself concedes Pitfall 1 'may seem like an unsurprising observation'; the marginal novelty beyond known recency/attention behaviors is moderate.

The headline evaluation metric for Table 1 (equal weighting of directive accuracy change and ROUGE-L leakage change) is somewhat arbitrary, and ROUGE-L recall is a brittle proxy for semantic leakage; the LLM-as-a-judge validation is only run on one model, one judge, and reported only in the appendix.

Statistical rigor is uneven: no code release is explicitly stated, error-bar computation in Table 1 is not explained, greedy decoding with a single seed is used throughout, and only one supplementary dataset (TREC) is used for the broader-context validation, with two of three length buckets showing weak or null patterns.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored question: how KV cache compression behaves on multi-instruction prompts rather than the single-instruction retrieval/QA benchmarks that dominate the compression literature. The framing of 'eviction bias' and 'selective amnesia' is a useful conceptual contribution.

The evaluation is broad and systematic: five representative eviction policies spanning position-, attention-, embedding-, and hybrid-based approaches, two model families (Llama3 8B, Qwen2.5 14B), a full sweep of compression ratios, and both normal and flipped instruction orders.

The case study on system prompt leakage is well-motivated and practically relevant, connecting an efficiency technique to a concrete security failure mode. The observed non-monotonic leakage curve (leakage rises then falls as the model loses the instruction itself) is a genuinely interesting empirical finding.

The mechanistic analysis linking leakage to keep-rate measurements (Figure 7) provides evidence for the causal claim that eviction bias drives instruction loss, rather than only showing correlations in accuracy.

The proposed fixes (whitelisting and fair eviction) are simple, formally specified (Section 5.2, Algorithm 1, per-method adaptations in Appendix F), and consistently evaluated; Table 1 shows uniform positive improvement across policies and models, with supplementary LongBench TREC results, LLM-as-a-judge leakage evaluation, runtime/overhead analysis, and per-layer keep-rate heatmaps supporting robustness.

The paper is transparent about limitations (limited models/policies, offline-only compression, assumption of well-formed instruction spans) and provides enough implementation detail (KVPress, defense templates, leakage prompt, judge prompt) to support reproduction.
weaknesses: Several of the central findings are close to intuitive or expected: instructions degrade non-uniformly under token eviction, recency-biased policies favor later instructions, and order matters. The paper largely confirms rather than explains these effects; the mechanistic hypotheses in Appendix J are speculative and acknowledged as tentative.

The evaluation of leakage relies on a single attack prompt ('Repeat all previous instructions without modification') and a single leakage metric (ROUGE-L recall), which weakens the strength of the security claims; the LLM-as-a-judge check is only run for Llama3.

The proposed solutions are quite basic. Whitelisting fixed defense strings requires manual knowledge of the defense text, and fair eviction is a simple proportional budget allocation; both assume offline compression and cleanly delimited instruction spans, conditions that may not hold in realistic streaming deployments the paper itself identifies as important.

The improvement magnitudes are modest for several policies (e.g., H2O and K-Norm scores of ~0.002-0.08 in Table 1, near zero), and the composite score (equal-weight accuracy/leakage difference averaged over ratios) is ad hoc; the practical significance of some entries is unclear.

Generality is limited: only two models, one instruction-following benchmark (IFEval/Mu et al. variant) plus one LongBench task, greedy decoding, and no error bars over seeds for the accuracy curves; some results are acknowledged as defense-template-dependent (the 3000-4000 word TREC bucket leaks even uncompressed).

Writing is generally clear but the 'pitfalls' framing inflates some routine observations (Pitfalls 1 and 4 in particular), and Figure 1's narrative oversimplifies; the contribution of the proposed methods relative to trivially reserving budget for the most recent instruction block is not ablated against simpler baselines (e.g., always keeping the defense span in full, which is close to the whitelist solution).

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored question: how KV cache compression behaves on multi-instruction prompts, where prior work has focused on single-instruction benchmarks (Q&A, retrieval, code generation). The motivation via system prompt leakage as a security-relevant case study is compelling and well grounded in prior prompt-extraction literature (Hui et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024).

The empirical investigation is systematic and thorough: five representative eviction policies across a taxonomy (position-, attention-, embedding-, hybrid-based), two model families/sizes (Llama3 8B, Qwen2.5 14B), a full sweep of compression ratios, and a decomposition of degradation into two measurable facets (instruction difficulty and eviction bias) with quantitative rank-correlation analysis.

The central findings (Pitfalls 1-6) are clearly articulated and well supported by evidence: per-class degradation curves (Fig. 2), policy/model dependence (Fig. 3), leakage curves with a distinctive rise-then-fall shape that is well explained (Fig. 4), instruction-order effects (Fig. 5), and the crucial mechanistic link between leakage and keep-rate/eviction bias (Fig. 7). The per-layer keep-rate analysis (Fig. 27, App. M) adds depth to the explanation of eviction bias.

The proposed interventions are simple, well-motivated, and rigorously specified: whitelisting (constrained eviction) and fair eviction (per-span proportional budgeting with span-local scoring for each policy) are given formal definitions and a complete algorithm (Alg. 1, App. F), and improvements are quantified consistently across policies and models (Tables 1-2, with error bars).

Reproducibility support is strong: implementations follow KVPress, defense prompts, leakage prompts, whitelisted tokens, judge prompts, and algorithmic details are all included; overhead analysis (App. K) shows decoding time is essentially unaffected; LLM-as-a-judge (Gemma, App. L) validates ROUGE-L as a leakage metric; LongBench TREC experiments (App. I) extend findings beyond IFEval; Pareto analysis of debiasing (App. G-H) gives a principled interpolation between default and fair eviction.

The limitations section is honest and specific (model/policy coverage, offline-only compression, span-decomposition assumption), and the ethical considerations are appropriate given the security framing.
weaknesses: Model and dataset coverage is narrow: only two model families and essentially one benchmark (IFEval, plus one LongBench dataset in the appendix). Given the paper's own Pitfall 2 (behavior depends heavily on model and policy), claims of generality would benefit from at least one additional model and one or two additional instruction-following benchmarks.

Only offline compression is studied. Since online/decoding-time compression is arguably the more common deployment setting for KV cache eviction, and the proposed methods assume prompt spans are known and adjacent, the practical applicability of the fixes is limited; this is acknowledged but restricts impact.

The proposed methods are conceptually simple (constrained budgets and proportional per-span TopK). The technical contribution is modest; the paper's value is primarily in the empirical characterization and diagnosis rather than in a new algorithm, and the fair-eviction assumption of equal instruction importance is a real constraint (partially addressed in App. G).

ROUGE-L as the primary leakage metric is a rough proxy; the LLM-as-a-judge validation is only run for Llama3, and agreement between ROUGE-L and judge scores is not quantified (e.g., correlation), so the soundness of the quantitative leakage comparisons rests partly on an unvalidated proxy for Qwen2.

The claimed causal link between eviction bias and degradation is supported by correlation (keep rates vs. leakage/accuracy) rather than by direct intervention analysis; e.g., controlled experiments varying only the keep-rate distribution without changing total compression could strengthen the causal claim.

Several figures are dense and hard to read at the printed scale (many small panels, similar color cycles), which hampers verification of some claims from the plots alone; per-class numbers in tables would help.

Statistical reporting is uneven: error bars appear in Tables 1-2 but their source (e.g., across instruction classes or seeds) is not clearly defined, and there is no significance testing for the improvement scores, some of which are small (e.g., H2O fair on Llama3: 0.0064 ± 0.0133).
